storyboard.claim: Mark proves to Will that the script of revenge has no final act.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark facing Will in the elevator, cold and certain — not comforting, exposing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Mark has been acting as director exposing Will's script; now he delivers the fatal line.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk signals Mark's narrative distance — he is not sad about this, he is demonstrating it.

storyboard.claim: Each act of revenge spawns the next; the credits never roll.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-step chain showing each shooting triggers the next — the loop has no exit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Mark just said it's never the end; the diagram makes the mechanism visible.
storyboard.addedInformation: The flow makes literal what the narration says abstractly: every sequel is built into the structure.

storyboard.claim: The rules sell revenge as closure when it is only the next link in the chain.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The three-rule list icon — the code of conduct that promises what it cannot deliver.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The flow showed the endless cycle; now the rules icon names the institution behind the lie.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike marks the false promise — the rules SAY this but the flow diagram just proved otherwise.

callout.text: holding the gun gives him control

storyboard.claim: Will believes the gun gives him authorial control over his own story.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will stands with a self-assured smirk — the false confidence of a boy who thinks he is the director.
storyboard.onScreenText: holding the gun gives him control
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After exposing the rules' false promise, we pivot to Will's own false belief.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: smirk signals the delusion without yet naming it false — the next beat will strike it.

callout.text: extra in a script by dead men

storyboard.claim: Will is not the director; he is an extra in a script written by dead men.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The puppeteer icon — dead men's hands pulling the strings — next to Will's blank, apathetic face.
storyboard.onScreenText: extra in a script by dead men
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Will's smirk of control collapses; the puppeteer shows who actually holds the strings.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank expression reads as apathy/numbness — he is already being moved, not moving.

storyboard.claim: A second mechanism beyond the ghosts applies intense, suffocating pressure from inside the book's own form.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will slumping in the elevator under invisible weight — the fear is physical, crushing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from the ghost argument to the formal/poetic pressure the verse form creates.
storyboard.addedInformation: Slump conveys the pressure as a bodily sensation, matching the narration's word 'suffocating'.

callout.text: verse form as a ticking clock

storyboard.claim: The book's free-verse form is literally a ticking clock — each sparse stanza eats one more second of the sixty-second ride.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The clock icon beside Will's frightened face in the elevator.
storyboard.onScreenText: verse form as a ticking clock
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the mechanism the previous beat introduced as suffocating pressure.
storyboard.addedInformation: Clock reads as time and deadline — exactly what the verse form enforces on the reader.

storyboard.claim: The verse is not standard prose; the words are radically sparse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will thinking in an abstract white set — the sparse page around him mirrors the description.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what the ticking-clock verse form looks like on the actual page.
storyboard.addedInformation: Abstract set reinforces the white-space description without needing a literal book prop.

storyboard.claim: A page might hold only three stacked repetitions of 'Shawn's dead,' surrounded by vast white space.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will slumped, Shawn's ghost faint beside him — the repeated loss filling almost nothing on the page.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes concrete the spareness just named — three words, a void, and a ghost.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shawn's ghost presence makes the repetition feel like the white space is his absence.

storyboard.claim: The white space and verse form are not an aesthetic gimmick — they are load-bearing structure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will in thought, abstract set — the narration making a structural argument about the book's form.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the white space established in the previous beat from style to structure.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: 'essential engineering' is the narrator's thesis; the staging simply holds it.

storyboard.claim: Prose is too comfortable and continuous to carry this story's speed and weight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will in contemplation — the abstract set holds the analytical comparison between prose and verse.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Having called it essential engineering, now explains why prose fails where verse succeeds.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: this is the narrator's reasoning beat; staging carries it through thought pose.

storyboard.claim: The short stanzas and abrupt line breaks force the reader to take the story in sharp gasps, not flowing sentences.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will afraid in the elevator — his tight, controlled breathing is the gasp the verse enforces.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the prose-vs-verse comparison: prose flows, verse gasps.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid expression in the room set makes the gasp physical — the body IS the verse form here.

storyboard.claim: The verse form IS the literal ticking clock of the sixty-second elevator ride.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The floor-counter icon above the elevator doors — the countdown Will watches while the stanzas tick by.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings together the verse-as-gasp and the elevator countdown into one image.
storyboard.addedInformation: FloorCounter is the book's own clock — more specific than a generic clock icon for this argument.

storyboard.claim: Reading the verse is like watching the typing bubble in a high-stakes argument — staring at the space, dreading what comes next.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will frozen, eyes wide, waiting — the tension before the blow lands.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sharpens the ticking-clock feeling with a visceral analogy the viewer can feel.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid + think = dread not curiosity — the wait is not anticipation but fear.

storyboard.claim: The physical box of the elevator mirrors the poetic constraints of the text.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will standing in the steel elevator walls — the tight frame IS the poetic constraint.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The clock / gasp / typing-bubble analogies culminate: physical space and poetic space are identical.
storyboard.addedInformation: Room set makes the elevator walls visible — the staging is the argument.

storyboard.claim: Reynolds' language is visceral and trapped in the body — 'tiny fists punching the backs of my eyes' instead of 'I held back tears.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will slumped, face sad — the body holding what words barely can.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Having argued the form is essential, now demonstrates it through a specific image.
storyboard.addedInformation: Slump shows held-in grief — the body IS the text's constraint made physical.

storyboard.claim: The language is trapped in the body just as Will is trapped in the elevator.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will slumped, the language-body metaphor made flesh — he cannot escape the words any more than the elevator.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the visceral image: fists in the eyes → language in the throat → body = cage.
storyboard.addedInformation: Same slump as previous beat reinforces the continuation of the argument — one long held breath.

storyboard.claim: Will is trapped in the elevator just as the words are trapped in the center of the page — a perfect alignment of form and psychology.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains icon beside Will in the elevator — bound, imprisoned, cannot leave.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The body-language-elevator triple mirror resolves: chains bind them all.
storyboard.addedInformation: Chains reads as bound and imprisoned — exactly the constraint the narration describes.

storyboard.claim: One host sees the white space as the emptiness of grief — the void where the dead used to be.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will and Shawn's ghost in the abstract void — the white space that surrounds them is the loss itself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from formal analysis to the emotional meaning of the white space.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shawn's ghost present makes the void tangible — the space IS him, absent.

storyboard.claim: The white space is the specific void left by each of the dead — Shawn, Danny, Pop.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Shawn and Pop as ghosts in the abstract white — their presence is the absence they name.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives names to the grief-void introduced in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Two ghosts from the cast embody the named dead — the white around them is the loss.

storyboard.claim: The second host acknowledges the grief-reading but signals a different, more unsettling interpretation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will in thought in the abstract set — a pivot point before the new reading arrives.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the grief reading and opens the threat reading — a hinge beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: this is a transition beat; staging holds space for the pivot.

callout.text: white space is the threat of violence

storyboard.claim: The white space is not passive grief — it is the active threat of violence waiting to erupt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will afraid in the abstract white — the space around him is no longer sad, it is dangerous.
storyboard.onScreenText: white space is the threat of violence
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly counters the grief-reading with the violence-reading — same image, new meaning.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid expression replaces the sad of the grief beats — the white space feels predatory now.

storyboard.claim: In a neighborhood with gun violence, the violence is not only the loud gunshot — it is the silence before and after.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will afraid on the street — the street set where the shooting happened, now quiet and tense.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the abstract white-space argument in the physical auditory environment of the neighborhood.
storyboard.addedInformation: Street set shifts from the elevator's interior — the outside world where the violence lives.

storyboard.claim: The violence IS the silence immediately after the shot, before the screaming starts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will frozen on the street — the moment the sound stops and the dread fills the air.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the specific silence that is violent — the gap between shot and scream.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid + idle = frozen in that silence — the body knows before the mind does.

storyboard.claim: The white space on the page IS that gunshot-silence — not grief, but violent threat.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will afraid in the abstract white — the equation is complete: page = street silence.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the loop from the street back to the page: the silence IS the white space.
storyboard.addedInformation: Return to abstract set mirrors the return to the page-reading argument.

storyboard.claim: The blank space around four words feels heavy, oppressive, like it is actively crushing the text.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will slumped in the white abstract set — the space around him pressing down.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes the violence of the silence physical — the white space has mass.
storyboard.addedInformation: Slump shows the crushing weight as a bodily sensation — the space is not empty, it is heavy.

callout.text: ghost in corners of the elevator

storyboard.claim: The white space is the ghost in the elevator corner — the suffocating rhythm of the rules pressing in.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The three-rules icon and Shawn's ghost in the corner of the elevator — the rules and the dead watch Will.
storyboard.onScreenText: ghost in corners of the elevator
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects white space, ghost presence, and the rules into one suffocating image.
storyboard.addedInformation: The rules icon ties the formal pressure back to the code — the silence the rules demand.

storyboard.claim: The silence — and the rules — demand to be filled with a gunshot, with retaliation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The gun icon beside Will, afraid — the weapon is the answer the silence is screaming for.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The suffocating white space finally names its demand — noise, retaliation, the gun.
storyboard.addedInformation: TheGun icon is the literal object the silence and rules point toward — the most direct visual.

storyboard.claim: The white space is the sixty seconds running out — the elevator is almost at the ground floor.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The floor counter above the doors counting toward L — time collapsing toward the moment of decision.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The formal/white-space argument resolves into the structural countdown — form and plot merge.
storyboard.addedInformation: FloorCounter is the book's literal clock; its appearance here marks the end approaching.

storyboard.claim: The elevator reaches the lobby — the end of the line. The match goes out. The heavy metal parts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will frozen in the elevator as the doors begin to open — the moment of irreversible arrival.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The countdown lands — elevator hits L, the sixty seconds are up.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid expression in the room holds the dread of the threshold — what is beyond the doors is everything.

callout.text: ghosts step out of the elevator

storyboard.claim: Every ghost — Buck, Dani, Mark, Pop, and finally Shawn — steps out of the elevator into the lobby.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Shawn and Mark walking out, sad — the ghosts departing together, leaving Will behind.
storyboard.onScreenText: ghosts step out of the elevator
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The doors opened; now the ghosts leave — the cross-examination disbands.
storyboard.addedInformation: Walk action is literal departure — the ghosts are no longer beside Will.

storyboard.claim: The ghosts turn and look back at Will. The jury rests. The book just stops.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will afraid, Shawn looking back at him — the two-shot holds the verdict in silence.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The ghosts walked out; now they turn — Will faces the jury of his own dead.
storyboard.addedInformation: TwoShot puts Will and Shawn in the same frame — the final confrontation, eye to eye.

storyboard.claim: Shawn asks two words — 'You coming?' — and Reynolds refuses to tell us what Will does.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Shawn pointing back toward Will — sad, not commanding — the question that ends the book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the jury looks back, Shawn speaks — two words, the whole book distilled.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sad expression on Shawn: not coercion, not demand — a brother asking, not a rule demanding.

storyboard.claim: Reynolds refuses to tell us whether Will walks out to kill Rigs or stays and puts the gun down.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The gun icon beside Will, afraid — the weapon is the entire unresolved question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shawn asked 'You coming?' — now the two possible answers are held in the gun's weight.
storyboard.addedInformation: TheGun is the object both answers hinge on — to carry it out or set it down.

storyboard.claim: Resolving the plot would completely undo everything the text just achieved.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will blank in the elevator — indifferent to an imposed resolution, stripped of the earned ambiguity.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The refusal to answer is introduced; now the narrator explains WHY the refusal is correct.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank expression = the apathy of a resolved story — the lesson that killed the meaning.

storyboard.claim: Giving Will a neat answer reduces a profound psychological exploration to a cheap morality play.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will blank in the abstract — the hollow result of a resolved story with a lesson.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the specific failure mode if Reynolds had given the 'good' ending.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank reads as apathy/indifference — the numbness of a story that asks nothing of the reader.

storyboard.claim: The after-school-special version — 'kids, put the guns down, violence is bad' — is exactly the cheap resolution the narrator rejects.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will blank, emptied of everything — the story that learned a neat little lesson and went home.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Satirizes the preachy good-ending: strike shows the narrator throwing this framing out.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike on 'neat little lesson' signals mockery — the narrator is rejecting this version of the story.

storyboard.claim: The other bad ending — Will shoots Rigs, it becomes a nihilistic tragedy, the ghetto is hopeless.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will slumped on the street, blank — the defeated, hopeless version of the story.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After rejecting the preachy good ending, now rejects the nihilistic bad ending.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike marks the narrator's rejection of this framing as much as the other; slump shows the collapse.

storyboard.claim: The nihilistic version says violence is inevitable — we feel sad and move on. The narrator rejects this entirely.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will blank on the street — the story that concluded nothing matters and closed the book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends and completes the nihilistic-ending critique from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike is the narrator's explicit refusal — this reading is as wrong as the morality-play version.

callout.text: the choice belongs to the reader

storyboard.claim: The choice must belong to Will — and by extension to the reader. We must sit with the unresolved weight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will surprised in the elevator — the revelation that the story's unresolved ending is a gift, not a failure.
storyboard.onScreenText: the choice belongs to the reader
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After rejecting both false endings, names why: the choice is the reader's burden and right.
storyboard.addedInformation: Surprised expression marks the shift from dread to revelation — the open ending is the point.
